title: One great body
hookLine: we are members of one great body; nature made us kin (Letters 95)
last: LIBERALIA STUDIA — WHAT IS IT FOR.

cards: Stub your toe and your whole body reacts. Your hand reaches down, your face winces, your other foot takes the weight. Nobody holds a meeting.
Nobody says: not my department, I'm a hand. The parts just know they belong to each other. The ninety-fifth letter is a long, dense argument about rules and principles in ethics.
Near the end, Seneca stops arguing and offers Lucilius a single formula for how to treat every other human being. It begins with the body.

teach.b: In Latin: membra sumus corporis magni. We are the limbs of one great body. Everything you see, divine and human, Seneca says, is one, and we are members of it.
Nature made us relatives, since she made us from the same materials and for the same ends. She gave us a love for one another and made us fit for living together. She set up fairness and justice.
By her law, it's worse to harm than to be harmed.

teach.h: NOTHING HUMAN IS FOREIGN TO ME.
teach.b: Then a line from the Roman playwright Terence, which Seneca tells Lucilius to keep on his lips and in his heart: I am human; I count nothing human foreign to me. Whatever happens to any person is my concern.
Our life together, he says, is like an arch of stones, which would fall if the stones didn't hold each other up. That's how it stands at all.

Stoic teachers had a word for this widening belonging, oikeiosis: care that starts with your own body can grow, they taught, to take in the whole human race. A stranger at a bus stop is a stone in your arch.

how: Stoic practitioners sometimes picture widening circles of concern, from self to family to strangers to all people, and act on that by helping someone they don't know.

o: a Stoic word for caring only about yourself first
a Stoic word for belonging that widens to all people
a Greek word for a household and its private property

games.q: a stranger drops a bag of groceries in front of you. you're in a hurry. what does the ninety-fifth letter say about who they are to you?
o: a stranger, so not your concern.
a fellow limb of one great body.
games.why: Seneca says we're members of one great body; like stones in an arch, we stand only by holding each other up.

practice: Feel your own body for a moment, hands, feet, the breath moving through the middle, all of it working together without being asked.

Then widen the circle: someone you love, someone you see often but barely know, a stranger far away waking up or going to sleep right now. Same materials, same breath; hold the whole widening circle as one body.

wordCard.voice: Oikeiosis. The Stoic word for a widening belonging: care that starts with your own body can grow to take in the whole human race. Today's word.
